Senses.Explanation: To hold fast is to keep something firmly in hand or under control. Chan records characteristically load the verb against ‘release or let go’ (放行): the two can name opposed exercises of authority, yet Wansong also says each can operate inside the other, so neither word fixes one outcome by itself. The compound has 773 exact hits in 203 files representing 199 independent works, and the contiguous pair ‘hold fast and release’ (把定放行) occurs 16 times in 14 files representing 14 works. Wansong quotes the saying, ‘when held fast, true gold loses its color; when released, rubble shines’ (把定真金失色，放行瓦礫生光), and calls this ‘having capture and release, able to kill and bring to life’ (謂之有擒有縱，能殺能活). Xuedou preserves the same opposition: ‘when released, rubble shines; when held fast, true gold loses color; the authority is in hand, killing and bringing to life accord with the occasion’ (放行則瓦礫生光，把定則真金失色，權柄在手，殺活臨時). These lines contrast true gold and rubble under holding and release; they do not by themselves define gold as enlightenment or establish one symbolism for gold elsewhere. The common objects show the physical pressure retained by the verb: ‘hold heaven and earth fast’ (把定乾坤), ‘hold the world fast’ (把定世界), ‘hold the key crossing’ (把定要津), and ‘hold the throat’ (把定咽喉). Hongzhi calls ‘holding the throat’ the work of a good hand in commenting on an exchange. In a recorded question, Jiufeng is asked ‘what is the eye that holds heaven and earth fast?’ (如何是把定乾坤眼) and answers, ‘heaven and earth are inside it’ (乾坤在裏許), then identifies that as the heaven-and-earth eye (正是乾坤眼). Wansong elsewhere says one eye ‘is also called the eye that holds heaven and earth fast, continuously leaking not the slightest thread, and is also named the diamond eye at the crown’ (一隻眼又喚作把定乾坤眼，綿綿不漏絲毫，亦名頂門具金剛眼).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue: Writing to Lü Juren, Dahui Zonggao calls the point at which there is no handle available to grasp good news and tells him not to fear falling into emptiness.

Senses.Explanation: To grasp is to seize something mentally or keep it under control; Chan records characteristically bring the verb to the point where no stable handle can be held. They also criticize the deliberate attempt to restrain thoughts, so the word names both the attempted grip and its failure without becoming a second thing. Zhaozhou Congshen calls grasping dreamlike empty flowers wasted labor. Linji Yixuan gives the attempt a sharper institutional setting: he rebukes people who seize and restrain arising thoughts while seeking quiet. Zhongfeng Mingben records being unable to hold steady amid drowsiness and distraction, yet locates no external obstruction there. Elsewhere he warns that turning 'no need to grasp' into a fixed explanation is itself another dreamlike construction. Sengcan’s verse says that dreamlike empty flowers need no grasping and pairs this with releasing gain and loss, right and wrong. Dahui Zonggao calls the moment when no handle is available to grasp 'good news.' The corpus therefore does not make grasping a literal seizure in these witnesses. It repeatedly uses the ordinary action of taking or controlling for attempts to secure thoughts, sayings, or an intelligible foothold, and it records the failure of that attempt.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.
